clue.text: A master of light farce with point to get across

parts.note: Ben Travers wrote the Aldwych farces of the 1920s
a compass point, east

explanation.surface: A comic playwright with a message he wants the audience to grasp.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole opening phrase names one man, the farce writer Ben Travers; the point is not a joke's point but a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: To traverse a place is to cross it from one side to the other, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Petty quarrel at home making midday meal

parts.note: a tiff is a small quarrel
being in is being at home

explanation.surface: A minor domestic row breaks out over lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiffin is an Anglo-Indian word for a light lunch.

clue.text: A coin for each person

parts.note: taken as written
a coin is a piece, as in a fifty-pence piece

explanation.surface: A coin is handed to every individual.
explanation.definitionFit: Apiece is an adverb meaning to or for each one.

clue.text: Agree, oddly, with bearded man, one volunteering for extra work

indicators.note: done oddly means in a strange way, so the letters come out strangely ordered

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
beaver is old slang for a man with a beard

explanation.surface: A man with a beard strangely agrees to take on overtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like it wants the odd letters, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An eager beaver is an over-keen person who volunteers for more work than needed.

clue.text: Dickens character, strong man securing power with money

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so one piece holds the other inside

parts.note: the biblical strong man
P is the abbreviation for power
brass is slang for money

explanation.surface: A Dickensian figure is a muscleman who holds power through wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dickens spelling has a P that the biblical hero's name lacks, which is where the power goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sampson Brass is the crooked lawyer in Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop.

clue.text: Wrong answer for peninsula

parts.note: a wrong, as a noun, is an offence
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Someone gives an incorrect reply when asked to name a peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' reads as an adjective on answer, but it is a noun meaning an offence.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crimea is the peninsula jutting into the Black Sea, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Letter from Greece from air hostess

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A flight attendant sends a letter home from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' suggests correspondence, but it is an alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rho is the seventeenth letter of the Greek alphabet, written like a P.

clue.text: Wholesale slaughter in Israeli port after religious ceremony

indicators.note: after says the port comes behind the ceremony in the word

parts.note: the Mass is the Eucharist service
Acre is a port on Israel's northern coast

explanation.surface: A news report of killings at a church service in an Israeli harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: A massacre is the indiscriminate killing of many people, slaughter on a large scale.

clue.text: City, Lincoln, run by university administrator, we hear

parts.note: Abraham Lincoln was known as Abe
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: we hear means what is said aloud, so the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: a dean heads a faculty

explanation.surface: A cathedral city is overseen by a college official.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln looks like the English city, but it is the US president.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberdeen is a city in north-east Scotland, an example of the category.

clue.text: Aunt Sally, perhaps?

parts.note: surface reading: an aunt called Sally, a relative
setter's reading: the traditional pub and fairground throwing game, and by extension anyone who is a legitimate target of attack

explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally is an old English throwing game played at fairs and pubs, in which sticks are hurled at a dummy's head; the figurative Aunt Sally is a person everyone feels free to criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a legitimate target for ridicule, and literally an Aunt Sally is a game played at a fair.

clue.text: Dessert — seconds accepted by timid type

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a mousy, timid person is called a mouse
S is the abbreviation for second(s)

explanation.surface: A shy diner happily takes a second helping of pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: The S goes in after MOU, giving MOU-S-SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A mousse is a light whipped pudding, often chocolate, served as a sweet course.

clue.text: Liqueur, one imbibed by imposing George Eliot character

parts.note: grand means impressive, imposing

indicators.note: what is imbibed is drunk in, so it goes inside

parts.note: Silas Marner, the weaver in her novel
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A grand character from a Victorian novel sips an orange liqueur.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside MARNER after the R, giving MARN-I-ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand Marnier is a French orange-flavoured cognac liqueur, a brand example.

clue.text: Suffer, popular course of remedial treatment incomplete

indicators.note: something incomplete is missing its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a cure is a course of treatment, as in a rest cure

explanation.surface: A patient endures a fashionable health regime that is never finished.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a loss or penalty is to suffer it, bringing it on oneself.

clue.text: Malibu, drab for us surprisingly

indicators.note: a surprising outcome is unexpected, so these letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone finds the glamorous California resort of Malibu unexpectedly dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Malibu looks like the place, but a malibu board is a long lightweight surfboard named after that beach.
explanation.definitionFit: A Malibu is a type of long surfboard, so the definition is an example of the answer.

clue.text: What some violent troublemakers wear for kicks?

definitions.text: What some violent troublemakers wear for kicks?

parts.note: surface reading: for fun, as a thrill

parts.words: What some violent troublemakers wear for kicks?
parts.note: setter's reading: heavy footwear worn by thugs for kicking people

explanation.walkthrough: 'For kicks' is the idiom for 'for fun', but here it is literal. Bovver is British slang for street trouble, and the heavy boots were associated with skinheads.
explanation.definitionFit: These are heavy laced boots worn by 1970s British skinheads, used as weapons in fights.

clue.text: Type of rhyme senior eleven composed

indicators.note: to compose is to put together into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The school's first cricket team wrote some rhyming lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonine verse is medieval Latin poetry in which the end of a line rhymes with a word at its middle.

clue.text: Frequently ring two newspapers

parts.note: O is ring-shaped
the FT (Financial Times) and The Times

explanation.surface: Someone is constantly phoning a pair of newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ofttimes is an archaic adverb meaning often, many times.

clue.text: Beverage teenager brewed

indicators.note: brewing mixes ingredients together, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A young person made a hot drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Green tea is a drink made from unfermented tea leaves, an example of a beverage.

clue.text: Novel author left out all the time, at first

indicators.note: at first places the time phrase at the front, before the writer

parts.note: constantly, always

indicators.note: out says something is removed, here the abbreviation for left

parts.note: Eric Ambler, the English thriller writer
L is the abbreviation for left; it is taken out

explanation.surface: A writer is constantly excluded at the start, perhaps of a book list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' could be an adjective meaning new, but it is the definition; 'at first' says the time phrase leads. Eric Ambler wrote spy thrillers such as The Mask of Dimitrios.
explanation.definitionFit: Forever Amber is Kathleen Winsor's 1944 bestselling historical romance, so it is an example of a novel.

clue.text: False rumour an eccentric put about

indicators.note: put about means placed around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a card is an eccentric or comic person
taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd character spread a piece of untrue gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put about' sounds like spreading a rumour, which suits the surface, but here it is the instruction to wrap one piece around the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is an unfounded story or hoax deliberately spread.

clue.text: In heart of Vietnam, blunder causes extreme fear

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

parts.note: the fourth of seven letters
an error is a blunder

explanation.surface: A war correspondent: a mistake deep in Vietnam leads to panic.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror is intense, overwhelming fear.

clue.text: The old one getting out of bed is a speculator

parts.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old
a riser is someone who gets up, as in early riser

explanation.surface: An elderly person climbing out of bed is a gambler on the markets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speculator' suggests money, but here it means someone who forms theories.
explanation.definitionFit: To speculate is to form theories without firm evidence, so a speculator in that sense is a theoriser.

clue.text: Daring support garment, extremely versatile

parts.note: a brassiere supports the bust

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word, its two ends

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A bold piece of underwear that can be worn many ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Brave and daring both describe someone willing to face danger, adjective for adjective.

clue.text: Spotted motorway leading to Yorkshire town

parts.note: M as in M1, the abbreviation for motorway
Otley is a market town in West Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A traffic report: something seen on the road into a Yorkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' reads as 'seen', but it is the adjective for something dappled or patchy in colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Motley means of many colours, like a jester's patched costume, so it fits spotted in that sense.

clue.text: Italian novelist in the city centre of Bologna

parts.note: EC is the postcode for the City of London

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the fourth of seven letters

explanation.surface: A writer is found in the heart of an Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, whose postcodes begin EC.
explanation.definitionFit: Umberto Eco wrote The Name of the Rose, so he is an example of an Italian novelist.

clue.text: Little known about Greek character, a monster

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: a minor figure is one of little fame
the Greek letter T

explanation.surface: A sea creature barely known to the Greeks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek letter goes between MINO and R.
explanation.definitionFit: The Minotaur is the bull-headed creature of Greek myth kept in the Cretan labyrinth, an example of a monster.

clue.text: Follow notice in programme

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: a television show is a programme
an advertisement, a notice

explanation.surface: Keep watching for an announcement in a broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: To shadow someone is to follow them closely and secretly, as a detective does.

clue.text: Champion eight reportedly unhappy about capsizing

indicators.note: reportedly means as said aloud, so the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: a rowing eight is a crew
sad means unhappy

indicators.note: a capsizing boat turns over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A champion rower is upset by the boat turning over.
explanation.walkthrough: A rowing eight is the boat's crew of oarsmen; 'eight' is a number in the surface but a team here.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusader is a campaigner who champions a cause, so champion works as a noun synonym.
